chapters.name: Intro
sentences: The seat belt sign comes on. Your drink starts to shake. And for a moment, the whole plane drops.
For many people, turbulence is the scariest part of flying.
But what is really happening outside the window? How strong is the plane? And who actually gets hurt?
Most of what people fear about turbulence is not true. But one part of it is very real.
In this video, we will follow turbulence from the sky, to the wing, to your seat.
And by the end, you will know the one simple habit that protects you most.

chapters.name: Air Is Like Water
sentences: Think of the air as an invisible ocean. It has currents, rivers and waves, just like water.
When a river flows smoothly, a boat glides. But where fast water meets slow water, or hits a rock, it starts to swirl.
Air does the same thing. When one layer of air moves faster than the layer next to it, the boundary between them breaks into swirls and eddies.
An airplane flying through those swirls is pushed up, then down, then sideways. That is turbulence.
The plane is not falling out of the sky. It is riding over bumps in the air, the way a boat rides over waves.

chapters.name: Where It Comes From
sentences: Turbulence has several main sources.
The first is heat. Warm air rises in columns, especially over land on sunny days, and inside thunderstorms those rising currents become violent. Pilots fly around big storms for exactly this reason.
The second is mountains. When strong wind blows across a mountain range, it can ripple downstream in huge waves, many miles long.
The third is other airplanes. Every wing leaves behind two spinning tubes of air from its tips, called wake turbulence. That is why planes take off and land a few minutes apart.
And the fourth is the most surprising one. It can happen in a perfectly blue sky, with no warning at all.

chapters.name: The Invisible One
sentences: It is called clear-air turbulence.
Pilots first started reporting it in the nineteen forties, as airplanes began to fly higher than ever before.
High above us flow the jet streams. These are rivers of fast wind, often hundreds of kilometres per hour, circling the planet.
At the edges of a jet stream, fast air rubs against slower air. The boundary breaks into swirls, exactly like the river we imagined.
It is most common between about twenty-three thousand and thirty-nine thousand feet. That is exactly where airliners cruise.
One study found that about two thirds of turbulence reports came from within about one hundred and fifty nautical miles of a jet stream's core.
The problem is that this air is clear. There are no clouds to see, and conventional weather radar cannot detect it.
So the first warning is often the bump itself.

chapters.name: How Strong Is the Wing?
sentences: Now, the question many nervous flyers ask. Can turbulence break the plane?
Engineers start with the strongest loads the airplane is ever expected to meet in service. These are called limit loads.
For an airliner, the design must handle at least two and a half times the force of normal gravity, pulling up.
The rules also include gusts of wind. At low altitude, the design must handle a sudden gust of fifty-six feet per second.
Then comes the safety margin. The rules say a factor of one and a half must be added on top of the limit load.
And at that higher load, called the ultimate load, the structure must hold for at least three seconds without failing.
Wings are not stiff. They are built to bend, so they can soak up the energy of a bump, like the springs in a car.
Each new airliner type is also tested on the ground, with its wings bent upward far beyond anything it should ever meet in service.
This is why, in normal airline flying today, turbulence very rarely damages the airplane itself.

chapters.name: What Pilots Do
sentences: Pilots fight turbulence long before you feel it.
Before departure, they study forecasts that show jet streams, storms and areas where turbulence is likely.
In the air, they listen to other crews. Pilots send short reports, called pilot reports, saying where they hit bumps, at what height, and how strong they were.
If the ride ahead looks rough, they ask air traffic control for a different altitude or a different route.
When they do fly through it, they slow to a special turbulence speed, which reduces the stress on the airplane.
And they switch on the seat belt sign. That small light is one of the most important safety tools on board.

chapters.name: Who Gets Hurt
sentences: So if the airplane is so strong, why is turbulence a safety topic at all?
Because people inside the plane are not as strong as the wings.
The United States safety board, the NTSB, studied ten years of airline accidents, from two thousand nine to two thousand eighteen.
It found that turbulence caused thirty-seven point six percent of those accidents. More than any other single cause.
In those ten years, one hundred and eleven turbulence accidents caused at least one serious injury.
And the people hurt most were not passengers. Seventy-nine percent of the seriously injured were flight attendants.

The FAA's own numbers tell the same story. From two thousand nine to two thousand twenty-one, it counted one hundred and forty-six serious turbulence injuries. One hundred and sixteen of them were crew members.
They are the ones standing up, serving drinks and pushing heavy carts, when the bump arrives.

chapters.name: When It Goes Wrong
sentences: Sometimes, the bump is severe.
In May twenty twenty-four, a long-haul jet flying from London to Singapore suddenly met severe turbulence.
Passengers and crew who were not strapped in were thrown against the ceiling. One passenger died, and dozens were injured. The jet diverted to Bangkok.
Events like this are rare, out of millions of flights every year. But they share one pattern.
The people who were badly hurt were mostly the people who were not wearing a seat belt at that moment.
In the early jet age, severe turbulence sometimes broke aircraft apart. Today, the danger is almost always to people, not to the plane.

chapters.name: Is It Getting Worse?
sentences: Many flyers feel that turbulence is getting worse. Scientists at the University of Reading checked.
In twenty twenty-three, they published a study that used forty years of atmospheric data, over the North Atlantic.
At an average point there, severe clear-air turbulence rose by fifty-five percent between nineteen seventy-nine and twenty twenty.
Moderate turbulence rose by thirty-seven percent, and light turbulence by seventeen percent.
The researchers link this to a warming climate, which is increasing wind shear inside the jet streams.
One of the researchers said the evidence suggests the increase has already begun.
But better forecasts are also coming. So more turbulence in the sky does not have to mean more injuries in the cabin.

chapters.name: How to Stay Safe
sentences: So what can you do? The answer is almost too simple.
Keep your seat belt fastened whenever you are sitting down, even when the sign is off.
Wear it loosely if you like. It only needs to stop you rising out of the seat.
Children under two years old are safest in their own seat, with an approved child seat, not on a parent's lap.
Store heavy bags under the seat in front of you, and close the bins above you.
And when the crew asks you to sit down, sit down quickly. They can often see what is coming before you can.

chapters.name: Outro
sentences: Turbulence is uncomfortable. But it is normal, it is expected, and the airplane is built for it.
The wings will bend. The coffee may spill. And with your seat belt on, you will almost certainly walk off the plane just fine.
So the next time the seat belt sign comes on, you will know exactly what is happening outside.
